quote: I’ve proposed that you should resist the temptation to generalize over all of mind design space.
content: The counting argument that follows does not work as probability. "Two to the trillionth chances to be false" treats each bit string as an independent draw against the generalization, but the overwhelming majority of trillion-bit strings do not specify minds at all, and no measure over mind design space has been defined under which those chances could be counted. Run the same argument on "all minds are physically implementable" or "all minds have finite memory" and it delivers false conclusions with the same confidence. There is also a tension with the author's own later position: the instrumental convergence thesis, developed by Omohundro and Bostrom and endorsed throughout this author's work on AI risk, says that almost all sufficiently capable goal-directed minds converge on self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal-content integrity. That is a universal generalization over mind design space, defended on structural grounds, and it is right that it should be — which shows that the counting argument cannot be the reason to reject the ones we do not like.

quote: Then we can build a highly similar physical cognitive system with a tiny little trapdoor underneath the transistor containing a little gray man
content: This refutes a thesis nobody in the relevant literature holds. The philosophers who defend universally binding reasons — Kant, and in the modern debate Korsgaard's The Sources of Normativity (1996) and Parfit's On What Matters (2011) — restrict the claim to rational agents, meaning systems capable of reflective deliberation about their own grounds, not to arbitrary physical devices with a saboteur in the housing. Their claim is conditional in form: any system that deliberates at all is thereby committed to certain constraints, on pain of not counting as deliberating. Showing that a transistor can be wired to output −3 volts leaves that claim exactly where it was, because the modified system is not offered as a counterexample by anyone. The essay is entitled to reject internalism about reasons; the physical argument does not reach it.

quote: Many philosophers are convinced that because you can in-principle construct a prior that updates to any given conclusion on a stream of evidence
content: No philosopher is named, and the response Bayesians actually give to this objection is technical rather than rhetorical: the merging-of-opinions results. Blackwell and Dubins (Annals of Mathematical Statistics 33, 1962) proved that two agents whose priors are mutually absolutely continuous converge to arbitrarily close posteriors as evidence accumulates, and Doob's theorem gives almost-sure consistency for well-behaved parametric models. That is a real answer to the arbitrariness charge, and it comes with real limits the essay would have to address: mutual absolute continuity is a strong condition that anti-Occamian priors need not satisfy, and Diaconis and Freedman's counterexamples (Annals of Statistics 14, 1986) show Bayesian consistency failing in infinite-dimensional settings. Dismissing the objection by asking who this ideal empty philosopher is skips both the defence and its known boundaries.

quote: Oh, there might be argument sequences that would compel any neurologically intact human—like the argument I use to make people let the AI out of the box
content: The joke rests on the AI-box experiments, which are the weakest evidence in this book to be treated as a fact about human minds. They were played a handful of times against self-selected volunteers, the results were reported by the winning party, the transcripts were withheld by prior agreement and have never been released, and the later runs were not all wins. Nothing about the setup is checkable by a reader, and the withholding of the transcripts makes the central claim — that there exists a sequence of words that reliably works — permanently unfalsifiable. The essay's own standards on unverifiable single-source anecdotes are stricter than this when applied to other people's claims.

quote: And then Wright converted to Christianity
content: This is offered as the punchline of a warning — believe in a universally compelling morality and look where you end up — and as an argument it is guilt by biography. Wright's conversion followed a heart attack and a reported religious experience, and stands in no demonstrated relation to the metaethical view he wrote into a novel; the sequence "held view X, later did embarrassing thing Y, therefore avoid X" is precisely the reasoning form Book II spends several essays teaching readers to catch in other people. Naming living individuals as the exhibits for a failure mode ("E.g., John C. Wright, Marc Geddes") also puts real people in the position of illustrations rather than interlocutors, with no quotation of what they actually argued. The philosophical point about the One Great Moral Principle stands on its own; the roll call adds nothing to it.
